notes.meaning: The prophet calls out to Lebanon, the northern entrance into the land, warning that an invading army will sweep through like fire. Lebanon's mighty cedar trees will be burned as the enemy advances toward Jerusalem. Many interpreters also see this as a picture of the temple itself, which was built with cedar from Lebanon and later destroyed by fire.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Ancient Jewish history and Catholic commentators noted that the massive temple gates swung open by themselves before the Roman siege, fulfilling the warning for Lebanon's doors to open.

notes.meaning: As the destruction moves south, lesser trees like the cypresses and oaks are told to weep because the mighty cedars have fallen. If the tallest and strongest trees cannot survive the fire, the smaller trees have no hope. In the same way, when a nation's rulers and great leaders collapse, ordinary people cannot escape the disaster.

The ruins spread down to the Jordan valley, where both human leaders and wild animals cry out in grief. Shepherds weep because their rich pastures are wiped out, and young lions roar because the river thickets where they lived have been ruined. This shows that the coming judgment spares no one, sweeping away proud leaders and humble lands alike.

God tells the prophet to act out the role of a shepherd caring for a flock doomed to die. This acted parable points to the Messiah, who came to guide and teach Israel even as national judgment drew near. God faithfully offered loving care to His people, even when their leaders were leading them toward destruction.

The sheep are mistreated by greedy buyers and sellers who slaughter them without feeling any guilt. These corrupt leaders even praise God for making them rich off the misery of their own people. The rulers who should have protected the flock felt no compassion for them at all.

Because the people hardened their hearts in sin, God announces that His mercy toward them has run out. He will hand them over to internal civil war and to the harsh rule of a foreign king, the Roman emperor. When that judgment falls, God will not step in to rescue them from the oppressors they chose.

The prophet obeys God and feeds the flock, paying special attention to the poor and humble who are willing to listen. He takes two shepherd staffs, naming one Favor to show God's protective grace, and the other Union to show peace among the tribes. This pictures how Christ came with tender care for the lowly, offering both divine favor and brotherly unity.

differ.view: The two staffs represent the preaching of the Gospel and the church ordinances that bind believers together.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: The two staffs represent two ways God deals with people: gentle mercy through kindness, and discipline or punishment when they stray.

notes.meaning: The shepherd gets rid of three corrupt rulers in a short time to protect the flock. Yet the people still despise the shepherd, and he becomes weary of their stubborn rebellion. This mutual grief shows how completely the people rejected God's loving direction.

differ.view: The three shepherds stand for the three offices of prophet, priest, and king, which were permanently dissolved when Israel rejected Jesus.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: The three shepherds may refer to three wicked kings in Jeremiah's day or three corrupt high priests deposed in quick succession.

notes.meaning: The shepherd finally gives up on the rebellious flock and leaves them to their fate. He removes his care, letting them fall victim to famine, war, and violent fighting among themselves. This came true when Jerusalem was besieged by Rome, and the starving people turned savagely against one another.

The shepherd breaks the staff called Favor, showing that God's special protection has ended. This covenant was God's restraint on foreign nations, which had kept them from destroying Israel. By breaking the staff, God removed His protective shield and allowed foreign enemies to attack the land.

God's protective covenant ended on that very day, just as He had said. The poor and humble among the people watched the prophet and recognized that this was truly the word of the Lord. Because they believed God's warning, this faithful remnant took heed and followed His guidance.

The shepherd asks the leaders to pay him whatever wages they think his pastoral service is worth. To insult him, they weigh out thirty pieces of silver, which was the legal price of an injured slave. This contemptuous payout showed how little they valued the shepherd, foreshadowing the thirty silver coins paid to Judas to betray Jesus.

The Lord speaks with bitter irony, calling the tiny payment a magnificent price placed on Himself. He commands the prophet to throw the insulting wage to the potter, and the prophet casts it down in the temple. This was fulfilled when Judas threw the betrayal money into the temple, and the priests used it to buy a potter's field.

The shepherd snaps his second staff, called Union, showing that the brotherly bond among God's people is broken. Once God's favor was removed, the nation fractured into hostile factions and bitter infighting. This deep division left the people helpless and ruined when the Roman army arrived.

The Lord tells Zechariah to put on the gear of a foolish shepherd. In the Bible, a fool is someone who acts wickedly and ignores God's law. Because the nation rejected the Good Shepherd, God would hand them over to abusive leaders who would harm them.

God warns that a cruel ruler will arise who refuses to do any of a true shepherd's work. He will not search for the lost, tend the young, heal the hurt, or support the healthy sheep. Instead, he will devour the choice animals and tear their hooves apart to take everything for himself.

differ.view: This foolish shepherd points ultimately to the future Antichrist, who will deceive the Jewish people and then treat them with great cruelty.

notes.meaning: God pronounces a curse on the worthless shepherd who abandons the flock in their time of need. A sword of judgment will strike his arm, which represents his power, and his right eye, which represents his wisdom. Because he refused to use his strength and sight to protect God's people, he is left completely powerless and blind.
